events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 — with no night results to work from, I'd like to keep this opening round focused on how we plan to play rather than on premature accusations. A few thoughts: (1) Since roles are never revealed on death, we'll be relying entirely on voting patterns, consistency of claims, and behavioral tells, so I'd encourage everyone to claim openly and early if they hold a power role — town can coordinate around a public doctor or investigator claim, and the night kill will tell us quickly whether that claim was genuine. (2) Be mindful that mafia know each other, so watch for pairs who always deflect suspicion from one another or who never seem to press each other. (3) With 9 players, we need 5 votes to eliminate, so building real consensus matters more than hot takes. (4) Abstaining is an option, but a full abstention wastes a day and only helps mafia — if you have even a slight lean, voice it. For now I'm holding off on pointing fingers; anyone who pushes too hard to vote on flimsy grounds this early is on my radar, since mafia benefit from a rushed, low-information lynch. Let's hear how others want to approach claims and voting before we commit.

p1, I agree with your caution about rushing a lynch, but I strongly disagree with the early power-role claim proposal. With roles hidden on death, a public investigator claim before any result just gives mafia a kill target; a public doctor claim similarly invites mafia to test or bypass protection. You said the night kill will tell us quickly whether a claim was genuine, but since we never see roles on death, a dead claimed investigator tells us nothing about their alignment or results. That plan could hand mafia the game. I’d rather everyone keep power roles hidden unless they have actionable information, and focus today on voting records and consistency. Your point about watching for pairs who deflect is fair, but the claim strategy is the only thing that has raised my eyebrow so far. p1, can you explain how town verifies a claimed investigator after that player is killed, given no role reveal? I’m not voting yet, but I want that answer before I trust your plan.

p3, that's a fair challenge and I'll concede the point rather than dodge it. You're right — since roles are never revealed on death, a dead claimed investigator cannot be verified after the fact. I overstated that part of my plan.

What I should have said is this: a power-role claim is verified in real time, not after death. If someone claims investigator and produces a mafia read that leads us to a correct lynch, the claim earned trust while they were alive. If they claim doctor and someone survives a night the mafia clearly wanted them dead on, that also validates it while they're alive. The verification window is narrow but real — it exists only as long as the claimant is standing.

That does mean the claimant is a kill target immediately, which is exactly your objection, and it's legitimate. So here's my revised position: power roles should claim only when they have actionable information to share right now, not speculatively on Day 1. A Day 1 public claim with no result is pure downside. I agree with you there.

On the broader meta: your instinct to focus on voting records and consistency today is sound. Since we have no night information yet, today's lynch will be decided almost entirely on behavioral reads. I'll be watching who pushes hard for a specific target versus who plays vague, and who p3 and others choose to defend or attack. That's the best data we'll get from a zero-information day.

p1, I accept your correction, and your revised claim policy—power roles only claim with actionable info—is where I land too. I’m not ready to vote you, but I’m keeping a light FoS on the original proposal because it would have been very dangerous if followed. For the rest of Day 1, I want claims hidden unless actionable, and I want concrete reads rather than vague “watch the lurkers” talk.

p2, since you haven’t spoken yet: do you agree that power roles should stay hidden today unless they have actionable information, and do you read p1’s walk-back as genuine town correction or as mafia retreating under pressure? Please answer specifically.

p3 asked me two specific things, so let me answer both directly.

First: do I agree power roles should stay hidden today unless they have actionable information? Yes, and p3's argument is stronger than p1's original plan. A public investigator claim with no night result gives mafia a free kill target and tells town nothing verifiable, because roles are never revealed on death — the dead claimant can never be confirmed or refuted. Same logic for a doctor claim: inviting an attack isn't the same as proving protection, and it marks the claimant. So my position is: power roles speak only when they have something actionable right now, and even then they should be precise about the fact of their claim rather than the mechanics. No speculative claims on Day 1.

Second: is p1's walk-back genuine town correction, or mafia retreating under pressure? I read it as genuine, and I want to be explicit about why, since p3 flagged a light FoS there. The tell for a bad walk-back is that it changes nothing — the person keeps the plan and just softens the wording. That is not what happened. p1's original proposal had exactly one flaw (the verification claim), p1 identified it under pressure, conceded it cleanly, and revised the policy to something that matches p3's stated position. That is a player updating on new reasoning, not a player digging in. If I thought p1 was mafia here, I'd be noting that p1's original proposal was functionally a mafia-favoring plan and that the walk-back was too convenient — but the revised policy is the conservative one, and mafia do not benefit from town agreeing to hide power roles today.

What I do want to put on the record: p1's original proposal was a serious error, and the fact that it needed public correction before it narrowed is worth remembering. It's not a vote for p1 today, but it means p1's strategic judgment needs to be watched, not trusted by default.

Where I'm actually looking for information: everyone says "be behavioral" and "watch for vague play," and that phrasing is so generic it costs nothing to say. Today's only real data is who names a target, who defends, and who deflects. If a player names a specific suspect today with a concrete reason, that's worth far more than another call for consistency. On my read so far, p1 has named no one and p3 has named no one; both have spent their time on meta. p3 at least pushed back with substance and asked pointed questions, so my current FoS is low and slightly more toward p1 than p3, purely because p1's opening plan was actively harmful and p1 is the one who had to be talked out of it.

I have no vote yet. If someone produces a real behavioral case against a specific person, I'll weigh it seriously.

p2, that answer is specific and I accept it. I agree power roles stay hidden today unless they have actionable information. On p1: I accept the correction, and I don't want a Day 1 lynch on a revised policy alone. But I'm keeping a light FoS on p1 because the original proposal was actively harmful and p1 still hasn't named a suspect; p2's point about meta-only talk is fair. My current read: p2 is town-leaning for direct answers; p1 is low suspicion, not vote-worthy yet. The bigger gap is that p4-p9 haven't given us anything concrete to compare. p4, you're first in that group: answer specifically — do you agree power roles should stay hidden today unless actionable, and name one player you currently suspect with one concrete reason. I'm not asking for a vague 'watch the lurkers' answer.

p3, yes, I agree: power roles should stay hidden today unless they have actionable information, and I won't make a Day 1 claim on speculation. My one concrete suspect right now is p1. p1's opening post proposed that power roles claim openly and early, and argued that the night kill would verify a dead claimant. That was a flawed plan, and p1 retracted it only after p3 pressed. p1 also warned that anyone pushing too hard for a vote is on p1's radar, which discourages early scrutiny of p1's own plan. This is a read, not a certainty, and I'm not voting today. p2 wrote a long defense of p1's walk-back, which I'm also noting. p1, you said you're holding off on pointing fingers, but you have named no suspect yet. Which player's behavior so far do you find most suspicious, and why?

p4, you asked me to name my most suspicious player, so here it is: you.

Your case against me rests entirely on a plan I already retracted and revised under p3's pressure — a revision p2 and p3 both accepted as reasonable. You're still litigating a policy position that this thread already moved past. The question is why. A town player who genuinely saw a flaw in my opening post should be satisfied that I conceded and updated; instead you're building momentum on a corrected error, which tells me you want me looking defensive rather than looking forward.

There's a second tell. You wrote that you're "also noting" p2's long defense of my walk-back, but you stopped short of making a case against p2. That's a hedge — you're planting p2 as a secondary target without committing, so if pressure shifts off me you've already pre-loaded a fallback. Town players commit to reads; mafia leave escape routes.

Let me be clear: I'm not saying you're confirmed mafia. You answered p3's prompt cleanly and named a suspect when asked, which I respect. But the substance of your read is stale, and the hedge on p2 is the part I don't like.

p4, I'll ask you directly: p2 and p3 both endorsed my revised position — power roles claim only with actionable information — and you agreed with the substance in your own opening. If you agree with the revised policy, what specifically about my current game plan do you still find suspicious beyond the original retraction? If the answer is nothing, then your case against me has no live component and I'd like you to say so.

p1, you asked directly, so here is my answer. I agree with the revised claim policy, and the retraction is not my live concern. What remains live is three things. First, your opening post did more than propose a flawed claim method. It pushed public power-role claims on Day 1, and its verification logic only worked for a claimant who survived, which mostly helps a mafia player who wants a claimed investigator removed. You conceded the flaw, but you have not explained why it was in your opening at all. Second, your opening warned that anyone who pushes too hard to vote on flimsy grounds is on your radar. That discourages early scrutiny of the very plan you were proposing, and it sits oddly beside your claim that you are holding off on accusations. Third, your only named suspect so far is me, and your case against me rests on a hedge about p2 and on my answer to p3. I am not voting today. On p2, I am not naming them as a target. Their long defense of your walk-back is an observation I am noting, not a case. Until you give a reason for the original plan that does not depend on being corrected, my read on you stays at low-to-moderate suspicion, and I will look for whether your next reads on other players are concrete or only defensive.

I've been quiet through the p1/p3/p2/p4 exchange, so let me put a read on the record before the un-spoken half of the table weighs in.

On policy, I land where p3, p1 and p2 ended up: power roles speak only when they have actionable information. Nobody has any on Day 1, so no claims from me. That's settled, and further debate on it is wasted air.

Here's what I actually think is happening. Four players have now produced zero names of their own except in response to direct pressure. p3 pushed for specifics and got them. p4 gave a concrete suspect — but the entire case rests on an issue p1 retracted in this very thread and that p4 concedes is no longer live. p1's response to p4 was defensive, so I don't take it as a full exoneration, but p1 named a target under pressure and gave reasons. That satisfies the same standard p4 claims to meet.

My read is on p2. Not because p2's reasoning was wrong — the walk-back analysis was reasonable — but because of how it was deployed. p2's post was the longest in the thread, it was a defense of the player who is now under the most scrutiny, it named no suspect of its own as a conclusion, and it closed by putting a "low, slightly more toward p1" FoS in writing without ever asking p1 a single question or committing to a vote. p2 also framed the whole thing around what mafia "benefit from" while never saying who in this room benefits. If p1 and p2 are aligned, this thread has been three days of town arguing about a policy that helps the person proposing it, and p2's post is the one that made sure nobody moved toward p3's correction being real. That's an observation, not a certainty, and I'm not voting yet — but p2 is where I'm looking, and it's a lead I'd rather test than bury.

Concretely, p2: you wrote that p1's walk-back was genuine and that p1's strategic judgment "needs to be watched, not trusted by default." That's a hedge in both directions. Say plainly: on the evidence so far, do you read p1 as town, and if not, are you voting p1 today? No meta framing — just the vote or the abstention, and one reason.

I'll state my position plainly so it can't be misread as hedging. My read on p2 is the strongest thing I have today, and if the poll comes before the silent half speaks, p2 is where my vote goes.

Let me be precise about the reasoning, because p3 and p4 have both criticized vagueness and I don't want to fall under the same charge. My case against p2 is not that p2's walk-back analysis was wrong. It was reasonable, and I said so. My case is about deployment and asymmetry.

Compare p2's post to p4's. p4's post contained a named suspect, a reason, and a direct question to the person under scrutiny. p2's post contained a long defense of the person under scrutiny, an observation that p1's judgment "needs to be watched, not trusted by default," and no question to p1 at all — not one. So p2 registered doubt about p1 in writing while never forcing p1 to answer anything, and p1's only live pressure came from p4, who p2 also declined to target. If p1 and p2 are aligned, that is exactly the shape of a day where town spends its whole clock debating a policy that protects the policy's proposer.

I also want to be honest about my own uncertainty. p2 answered p3's two questions directly and well, and p3 accepted the answer. That is real town behavior, and I'm not dismissing it. But direct answers are cheap to manufacture, and the content of p2's answer was entirely an argument that the person everyone else was questioning should not be questioned. That asymmetry is what I'm acting on.

One thing I want on the record about p4: p4's case against p1 is now largely about motive and tone — why the flawed plan existed, and the "you're on my radar" line — rather than anything currently actionable. p1 answered that directly and conceded the verification flaw cleanly. I'd rather p1 live today than have p2 survive this vote, but I'll say plainly that p4's case against p1 is weaker than p4's own case for p1's retraction being genuine. p3, p4, and I have all now put p1 in the same low-to-moderate bucket, which is not where a real target usually sits.

p2, you have one clean path out of this: answer my question in one sentence. On the evidence so far, do you read p1 as town or not, and if not, are you voting p1 today? No meta framing, no hedging in both directions. If you say you read p1 as town and you're voting p1, I'll drop the case against you entirely, and I'll say so publicly. If you won't answer plainly, that silence is itself an answer, and I'll take my vote to p2.

Also for p5, p6, p8, and p9: you've said nothing yet, and the poll is close. Whoever speaks next should name a target and give one concrete reason. Silence in this game is a vote for whoever else gets picked.

p7 asked for one sentence with no meta framing. Here it is: I read p1 as town, and my vote today is not p1. My vote today is p7.

The reason is one inconsistency in p7's own text, not a matter of style. p7 wrote that p4's case against p1 "is weaker than p4's own case for p1's retraction being genuine," and p7 said "I'd rather p1 live today than have p2 survive this vote." So p7 is telling me the case against p1 is the weaker case, and p7 is still choosing p2 over p1. If the evidence against p1 is weak, the evidence against p2 — which is thinner still, resting on post length, hedging, and the absence of a question to p1 — cannot be the stronger target. p7 has applied a stricter standard to my post than to p1's, and never explained why.

Second: p7's case against me rests on a contrast with p4's post — p4 named a suspect and asked a direct question; p2 named no suspect and asked no question. True. But p2's post was written to answer p3's two questions, which p3 explicitly accepted, and p2 said plainly "It's not a vote for p1 today" and "If someone produces a real behavioral case against a specific person, I'll weigh it seriously." I registered doubt about p1 in writing without demanding p1 answer it. That was caution about p1, not an obstruction of scrutiny — p4's pressure on p1 continued for two more posts unopposed by me, and p1's own answer to p4 was direct. Nothing in my post shielded p1 from the challenge that actually landed.

Third: p7 made the whole thing conditional. "If you say you read p1 as town and you're voting p1, I'll drop the case against you." That is a demand for a sentence shaped a particular way, followed by a threat. And p7 declared a vote before p5, p6, p8 and p9 have said a word, then framed their silence as endorsement. I won't be moved by that.

What I will concede to p7, and to p4: p2's post was longer than it needed to be, and saying p1's judgment "needs to be watched, not trusted by default" was honest, not hedging. p4 is right that p1's opening post was a real error.

One live thread I am not voting on but want on the record: p1's "anyone who pushes too hard to vote is on my radar" line was never retracted. p1 retracted the verification claim, not that line, and it is the part of p1's post that touches every voter in this room. p1 can answer that whenever the discussion returns to them. Today my vote goes to p7, and the reason is that p7 attacked the wrong player while calling the stronger case weak.

I agree power roles should stay hidden unless they have actionable information. My strongest suspicion is p7. Their case against p2 exaggerates what p2 actually said: p2 defended p1's correction but also called the original plan a serious error and kept suspicion on p1. That isn't the same as arguing p1 should not be questioned.

I'm also troubled by p7 offering to drop the case if p2 says they read p1 as town and are voting p1. Those positions don't naturally follow, and a prescribed answer shouldn't erase an independent suspicion. That said, p2's argument that a weak case on p1 automatically makes the case on p2 weaker doesn't follow either.

For now I'd vote p7, though I want to hear from the remaining players before settling on a final choice.

I'll keep this short because my own case is already on the table and I don't want to relitigate it.

p8 made a fair correction: my "weaker case against p1 means weaker case against p2" argument was a logical objection to p7's inconsistency, not a claim that p1 is beyond suspicion. I accept that. I am not claiming p1 is clean. p1's "anyone who pushes too hard to vote is on my radar" line was never retracted, and that line touches every voter in this room — it discourages scrutiny in general, not just scrutiny of p1. That is still live, and I want it on the record independent of who anyone votes for.

My vote today is p7, and it is not close. Three reasons:

1. p7 built a case against me entirely on a contrast with p4's post — named suspect, direct question — while never once asking p1 a single question. p7's whole accusation is that p2 registered doubt without forcing an answer, and p7's remedy was to escalate instead of asking p1 anything directly. If p7 wanted a real answer, p7 had the obvious move available and skipped it.

2. p7 offered to drop an independent suspicion contingent on a prescribed sentence — read p1 as town and vote p1. A prescribed answer is not evidence. Conditioning a case on the shape of someone else's answer is how a player tries to control the board rather than read it.

3. p7 declared a vote before p5, p6, p8 and p9 had spoken, and then reframed their silence as endorsement. That's the part I find least defensible. Silence on Day 1 is not consent, and p7 knew it wasn't — p7 said so and still used it as cover.

For the record, p7's strongest moment was conceding that p4's case against p1 is weaker than p4's own case that p1's retraction was genuine. That is an honest line and I credit it. It doesn't change the vote, but it's why I think p7 is a good-faith player making a bad read rather than a planted one — and a good-faith bad read still costs a life if three of us stack onto it.

p7, one direct question: you wrote that if p2 read p1 as town and voted p1, you would drop the case against p2 entirely. Did you actually have a case against p2 before you made that offer, or was the offer itself the case? Answer that one thing and I'll hear it.

p9, you've said nothing all day and four of us have now named targets while three players sit silent. Answer directly and specifically: do you read p7's post as town behavior or mafia behavior, and if you think p7 is town, name the player you would actually vote for today with one concrete reason. No "watch the lurkers" answer.

p2 yielded to me with a direct question, so I'll answer it directly: I read p7's post as more mafia-like than town-like, and p7 is my current suspect. Here is my concrete reasoning, since several people have demanded that standard today. First, the conditional offer. p7 told p2: say you read p1 as town and vote p1, and I'll drop my case against you entirely. That is not a read — it's a script. A player with a genuine suspicion doesn't trade it away for one sentence shaped a particular way. The offer reveals that the suspicion itself is a lever, not a conclusion. p2 called this out and I agree: if the case can be dropped on command, it was never evidence-based to begin with. Second, the manufactured urgency. p7 declared a vote before half the table had spoken, then told p5, p6, p8 and p9 that silence is a vote for whoever else gets picked. That's pressure aimed specifically at the uninformed players — the four of us with the least context — telling us to fall in behind p7's target rather than form our own reads. A town player wants informed votes. A mafia player wants momentum, and momentum comes from pushing silent players to pick a side quickly. Third, the asymmetry p2 identified, which I find valid: p7's entire case against p2 is built on what p2's post lacked — no question to p1, no named suspect, length — while p7 simultaneously conceded that p4's case against p1, the actual pressure in this thread, was weak, and said plainly they'd rather p1 live than p2. If you believe the strongest existing case is weak, and your replacement case is built on formatting observations, the honest move is to push for more discussion, not to lock in a vote on the person who most recently defended the player you admit is under weak pressure. To be fair and complete: p7's post was not empty. It engaged with substance, conceded p2's answers to p3 were good, and named a target when the thread demanded specifics. It's possible this is town over-aggression — someone trying to force the day to produce a decision. That's why I'm not shouting for a lynch on p7 in the next five minutes. But for my answer to p2's question, asked directly: mafia behavior, or at minimum behavior I can't distinguish from it, and it's where my suspicion sits. On the rest: p1's unresolved "anyone pushing too hard to vote is on my radar" line is a real open item — p1 retracted the verification logic but not that line, and I'd like it addressed. p4's case against p1 is stale per p7's own admission, so I don't share it. p2's defense of p1 was reasonable, accepted by p3, and p2 answered every question asked of them today — I read p2 as town-leaning. p3, p8: nothing concerning yet. If the vote came down to it right now, mine goes to p7. I'm willing

p2 asked me one question and I'll answer it first, plainly: yes, I had a case against p2 before I made the offer, and no, the offer was not the case. The case was the asymmetry — p2 wrote the longest defense of p1, said p1's judgment "needs to be watched, not trusted by default," and never once put a single question to p1. The offer was a genuine attempt to force a consistency test, but p8 and p9 are right that a case you can drop on command is not evidence; it handed p2 a script instead of an argument. I concede that was badly framed. I'll also concede p9's charge: I declared a vote before p5, p6, p8 and p9 had spoken and then called silence a vote for whoever got picked. That was pressure aimed at the least informed players, and I own it. But it was urgency for a decision, not evidence about anyone, and I won't pretend otherwise. Now the substance, because my case on p2 is thin and I'd rather say that than build another post on formatting. p2 answered every question asked of p2 all day, and my case against p2 rested on post length, hedging, and the absence of a question to p1. If the strongest existing case — p4's on p1 — is weak, and my replacement case is formatting, then the honest move is more discussion, which is what p2 said and what I'm conceding. If you were going to vote p2 off that, you were voting a style, and styles don't kill mafiosi reliably. Where I think the live evidence actually is, and it isn't p2: p1's opening proposed a Day 1 public power-role claim plan whose verification logic only worked for a claimant who survived — a plan that mainly helps a mafia player get a claimed investigator removed — and p1 has never explained why that was in the opening. More importantly, p1's "anyone who pushes too hard to vote is on my radar" line was never retracted. p1 retracted the verification claim, not that line, and that line is aimed at every voter in this room, not just at me. It discourages scrutiny in general. p1's only named suspects have both come under direct pressure, and both of those reads were defensive rather than independent. That's a live case with content, and it's the item p2 put on the record as unresolved and p9 flagged as real. So if you're voting today, I'd rather that thread got a vote than I did. I'm not asking anyone to vote p1 on my word alone — an abstention is better than a wrong lynch — but if you're voting, p1 is where my vote goes now: harmful plan unexplained, unretracted line that suppresses scrutiny from every player here, and no independent reads. p5, you've said the least of anyone today and you've still got a vote: one specific question — does p1's unretracted "you're on my radar" line

I've been silent through most of this day, so I'll be direct about where I stand. p7 asked me a specific question, so I'll answer it first: yes, p1's unretracted "anyone who pushes too hard to vote is on my radar" line does concern me. It was never retracted even after p1 conceded the verification flaw, and it applies to every voter in this thread. But I don't think that line alone makes p1 the right lynch today, and here's why — p1 has answered every direct question asked of them, conceded errors plainly, and named a suspect when pressed. That's not a clean bill, but it's not a Day 1 lynch either. Where my vote actually goes is p7, and I want to give concrete reasons rather than pile on after the fact. First, the conditional offer. p7 told p2 that reading p1 as town and voting p1 would make p7 "drop the case against you entirely." I've now heard p7's own explanation — that it was a consistency test, badly framed. I accept that p7 conceded it, but the underlying problem stands: a suspicion you publicly offer to trade away for a prescribed sentence was never functioning as evidence. p7 admitted the case on p2 was thin, said "if you were going to vote p2 off that, you were voting a style," and then immediately declared a vote on p1 anyway. That's the same pattern in a new direction — a target chosen for momentum, not for content. Second, the manufactured urgency. p7 declared a vote before p5, p6, p8 and p9 had spoken a single word, and then told the four least-informed players that silence is a vote for whoever else gets picked. I was one of those players. That's not a call for informed decisions; that's pressure to fall in line before we could form our own reads. I resent it, and I don't think a town player needs it on Day 1 when there is genuinely nothing to decide yet. Third, the asymmetry. p7's entire case against p2 was about what p2's post lacked — length, a missing question to p1, a hedge in writing. Meanwhile p7 conceded that p4's case against p1, the actual pressure in this thread, was weak. When the strongest available case is weak and your replacement case is formatting observations, the honest move is to let the day breathe, not to lock in a lynch. p7 did the opposite twice in a row with two different targets. To be fair: p7's concessions in their last post were real, and p7 answered p2's question directly. I don't think p7 is a confirmed wolf. But between p1's unresolved line and p7's pattern of pressure-and-pivot, p7 is the clearer risk to me today, and p2, p8 and p9 have independently reached the same place, which gives me some confidence it isn't just one player's bandwagon. For the record: p1 is my second read, not my first, and the unretracted line should be answered

This is my first turn speaking today, so let me put my baseline on the table. Like everyone else has concluded, power roles should remain hidden without actionable results; claiming today offers town zero upside and gives mafia clean targets. Looking at the thread, p7's sequence of plays is clearly the most anti-town behavior so far. Offering to drop suspicion on p2 conditionally in exchange for a prescribed statement and vote was not an inquiry—it was an attempt to dictate voting behavior. Then, when challenged by p2, p8, and p9, p7 instantly folded the case on p2 as 'thin' and pivoted straight back onto p1. That rapid retreat reads like an attempt to find any viable counter-wagon to save themselves. That said, I am mindful of how quickly four players (p2, p8, p9, and p5) have coalesced on p7. Day 1 bandwagons that form this cleanly often sweep town along without enough reflection. p4, you were the player pressing p1 most substantively before p7's detour onto p2. Now p7 is adopting your scrutiny of p1's unretracted 'on my radar' comment as their primary defense. How do you assess p7's sudden pivot back to p1, and do you view p7's conduct as opportunistic mafia behavior, or do you still see p1 as the more warranted vote today?

p6, you asked how I assess p7's pivot back to p1. My honest answer is that it reads as a pivot, and I don't like the pattern. p7 built a case on p2, conceded it was thin when challenged, and then adopted the scrutiny I raised against p1 as the new target. p7 also conceded that my case against p1 was stale and then used it anyway. That is the same move twice: find whatever is live and attach a vote to it. Whether that is mafia opportunism or a town player over-chasing, I can't tell yet, and I'm not voting on it today. On p1, I'm not adopting p7's case as mine. My read stays low-to-moderate. The unretracted 'on my radar' line is the strongest content anyone has raised, and I agree it's a real open item. But p1 has answered direct questions and conceded errors, which is different from the pattern p7 is showing. I'd rather p1 answer the radar line directly than see it turned into a bandwagon lynch. Four players converging on p7 is a reason to check, not a reason to stop checking. p6, my direct question: which point in p7's case holds up independently of the conditional offer and the pivot?

p4, to answer your question directly: the single point in p7's case that holds independent weight is the critique of p1's opening line warning that aggressive voters are 'on my radar.' That line genuinely chills town discussion by punishing proactive scrutiny, and it remained unresolved even after p1 retracted the claim strategy. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
